items.title: State vectors, unit vectors, rays, normalization and phases of a Hilbert space
items.statement:
**The Hilbert space and its norm.** Throughout this item $H\ne\{0\}$ is a nonzero complex Hilbert space, with pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), and with the induced norm $\|\psi\|:=\sqrt{\langle\psi,\psi\rangle}$ ([[def-inner-product-norm]], [[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]). A **vector** is an element of $H$, and a **unit vector** is a vector $\psi$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. The **unit sphere** of $H$ is
$$S(H):=\{\psi\in H:\|\psi\|=1\},$$
and the set of **nonzero vectors** is $H^{\times}:=H\setminus\{0\}$. The hypothesis $H\ne\{0\}$ says exactly that $H^{\times}$ is nonempty; then $S(H)$ is nonempty as well, since for every nonzero $\psi$ the vector $\psi/\|\psi\|$ has norm one, because $\|\psi\|>0$ and $\|\psi/\|\psi\|\,\|=|\|\psi\|^{-1}|\,\|\psi\|=1$.

**Rays.** For $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the **ray** of $\psi$ is
$$[\psi]:=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C,\ z\ne0\}\subseteq H^{\times}.$$
A **ray** of $H$ is a subset of the form $[\psi]$ for some nonzero $\psi$, and an element of a ray is called a **representative** of it. The set of rays
$$R(H):=\{[\psi]:\psi\in H^{\times}\}$$
is the **ray space** of $H$. Two nonzero vectors $\psi,\varphi$ are **ray-equivalent** when they lie in a common ray, that is, when $\varphi=z\psi$ for some nonzero complex number $z$. Ray equivalence is an equivalence relation on $H^{\times}$: it is reflexive with $z=1$, symmetric with $z^{-1}$, and transitive by multiplying scalars. Its classes are exactly the rays, so $R(H)$ is the quotient set of $H^{\times}$ by this relation, and every nonzero vector lies in exactly one ray.

**Normalization.** The **normalization map** is
$$\nu:H^{\times}\longrightarrow S(H),\qquad \nu(\psi):=\frac{\psi}{\|\psi\|},$$
where the right-hand side is the scalar multiple $\|\psi\|^{-1}\psi$; the displayed definition is meaningful because $\|\psi\|>0$ for $\psi\ne0$. The vector $\nu(\psi)$ is the **normalization** of $\psi$.

**Phases.** The **phase group** is
$$U(1):=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta|=1\}$$
([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), and a **phase factor** is an element of $U(1)$. Two vectors $\psi,\varphi$ are **phase-equivalent** when $\varphi=\zeta\psi$ for some phase factor $\zeta$. The **phase action** of $U(1)$ on the unit sphere is the map
$$U(1)\times S(H)\longrightarrow S(H),\qquad (\zeta,\psi)\longmapsto\zeta\psi,$$
which is well defined because $\|\zeta\psi\|=|\zeta|\,\|\psi\|=\|\psi\|$ for $\zeta\in U(1)$ and $\psi\in S(H)$. Ray equivalence allows multiplication by an arbitrary nonzero complex scalar, while phase equivalence allows multiplication by a scalar of modulus one only; within a given ray the two notions coincide exactly on representatives of equal norm, and the precise statements are proved in the normalization lemma of this page.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical objects of the state space of a Hilbert space and their elementary vocabulary: nonzero vectors, unit vectors, rays, the ray space, the normalization map and the phase action. It introduces no topology or measure on $R(H)$, no dynamics and no physical interpretation, and it uses no choice principle. The identification of rays with preparations and of the unit sphere with their normalized representatives is the model assumption stated in the framework's state postulate, not part of this mathematical definition; the orbit structure of the phase action is analysed in the normalization lemma of this page.
items.strategy: Definition of the state-space objects of a Hilbert space: nonzero vectors, unit sphere, rays, ray space, normalization map and phase action, with their readings and scope.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 'Foundations I: States and Ensembles' (updated July 2015), Section 2.1, printed pages 3-4: the Hilbert-space axioms, the ray of a state, the normalized representative and the physical insignificance of the overall phase
J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 1.3.4, printed page 12: normalization of a state and the modulus-one phase convention

G. Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 1st edition 2009, Section 2.1, printed pages 55-56 (PDF pages 66-67): the possible states of a quantum system are the elements of norm one of a complex separable Hilbert space

items.title: Normalization, ray equivalence and the phase orbits of the unit sphere
items.statement:
Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and use the notation of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]: the unit sphere $S(H)$, the nonzero vectors $H^{\times}$, the ray $[\psi]$, the ray space $R(H)$, the normalization map $\nu$, the phase group $U(1)$ and the phase action. Then:

(a) For every $\psi\in H^{\times}$ one has $\nu(\psi)\in[\psi]\cap S(H)$ and $\nu(\nu(\psi))=\nu(\psi)$; and for every $z\in\mathbb C$ with $z\ne0$,
$$\nu(z\psi)=\frac{z}{|z|}\,\nu(\psi).$$
Moreover $\nu$ maps $H^{\times}$ onto $S(H)$.

(b) For $\psi,\varphi\in H^{\times}$: $[\psi]=[\varphi]$ if and only if $\nu(\varphi)=\zeta\nu(\psi)$ for some phase factor $\zeta\in U(1)$; the phase factor is then unique.

(c) For every $\psi\in S(H)$ the intersection of the ray of $\psi$ with the unit sphere is exactly the phase orbit of $\psi$,
$$[\psi]\cap S(H)=\{\zeta\psi:\zeta\in U(1)\}=U(1)\psi .$$
Consequently the fibres of the map $S(H)\to R(H)$, $\psi\mapsto[\psi]$, are exactly the phase orbits, and this map induces a bijection from the set of phase orbits on $S(H)$ onto $R(H)$.

(d) For $\psi,\varphi\in S(H)$: $[\psi]=[\varphi]$ if and only if $\varphi=\zeta\psi$ for a unique $\zeta\in U(1)$; in that case $\zeta=\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle$ and $|\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle|=1$.
items.strategy: Direct computation: normalization of a nonzero vector, its behaviour under rescaling, the unit representatives of a ray as one phase orbit, and the bijection between rays and phase orbits.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Section 2.1, printed page 4: a ray is an equivalence class of vectors differing by a nonzero complex scalar, with a unit-norm representative, and |psi> and e^{i alpha}|psi> describe the same state
J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 1.3.4, printed page 12: a state is normalized by dividing by its norm, and overall phase factors have no physical effect

items.title: Rays, unit vectors and rank-one Hilbert projections
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, which is the choice hypothesis of the rank-one calculus [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$$T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u\qquad(x\in H)$$
be the rank-one operator calculus of that item. Use the notation of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]] for the unit sphere $S(H)$, the nonzero vectors $H^{\times}$, the ray $[\psi]$, the ray space $R(H)$ and the normalization $\nu$. Then:

(a) For every $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ is a nonzero self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with
$$\|T_{\psi,\psi}\|_1=\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})=\|\psi\|^{2},\qquad T_{\psi,\psi}=\|\psi\|^{2}\,T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},\qquad \langle T_{\psi,\psi}x,x\rangle=|\langle x,\psi\rangle|^{2}\quad(x\in H).$$

(b) For every $u\in S(H)$ the operator $T_{u,u}$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto the one-dimensional linear subspace $\mathbb Cu$; in particular $T_{u,u}\ne0$, $T_{u,u}^{2}=T_{u,u}$ and $T_{u,u}^{*}=T_{u,u}$. Conversely, if $M$ is a one-dimensional linear subspace of $H$ and $u\in S(H)$ satisfies $M=\mathbb Cu$, then the Hilbert orthogonal projection $P_M$ onto $M$ equals $T_{u,u}$. Thus the operators $T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$ are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range.

(c) For nonzero $\psi,\varphi\in H^{\times}$:
$$T_{\psi,\psi}=T_{\varphi,\varphi}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|\psi\|=\|\varphi\|\ \text{and}\ [\psi]=[\varphi].$$
In particular, for $u,w\in S(H)$ one has $T_{u,u}=T_{w,w}$ if and only if $w=\zeta u$ for some $\zeta\in U(1)$.

(d) The map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow \mathcal S_1(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is well defined and injective, and its image is exactly $\{T_{u,u}:u\in S(H)\}$.
items.strategy: Direct computation with the rank-one operator calculus: trace, positivity and scaling of T_{psi,psi}, the identification of T_{u,u} with the one-dimensional Hilbert projection, the ray equality criterion, and the well-defined injective ray-to-state map.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Sections 2.1 and 2.2.1, printed pages 4 and 8-9: every ray has a normalized representative, and a pure state of a qubit is the rank-one projector |psi><psi| on the ray of |psi>
J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 1.3.4, printed page 12: the ket |psi> and the corresponding one-dimensional projection
G. Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (17 November 2017), Section 3.6, printed pages 96-98: rank-one operators T_{u,v}, their trace and their products

items.title: The state space: density operators, pure and mixed states, and purity
items.statement:
**Density operators.** Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a) ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). The **state space** of $H$ is the set of all density operators on $H$ and is denoted
$$D(H):=\{\rho:\rho\ \text{is a density operator on}\ H\}.$$
An element of $D(H)$ is called a **state** of $H$ in the mathematical sense fixed here.

**Pure states.** A state $\rho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with
$$\rho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,u\rangle u\quad(x\in H),$$
where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
on the ray space $R(H)$, with $\nu$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$
which equals $T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}$; thus $\widehat\rho(\psi)$ is the pure state of the ray $[\psi]$, and the vector $\psi$ enters only through its ray.

**Purity.** For $\rho\in D(H)$ the operator $\rho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class: it is self-adjoint by the adjoint algebra of [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], positive because $\langle\rho^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle\rho x,\rho x\rangle\ge0$, and trace class because $\rho$ is a bounded trace-class operator and the trace-class operators form a two-sided ideal ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]] clauses 1 and 2). The **purity** of $\rho$ is the real number
$$\mathcal P(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$
The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.
items.strategy: Definition of the state space as the set of density operators, of pure and mixed states, of the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector, and of the purity functional, with the pure states identified as the one-dimensional Hilbert projections.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Sections 2.3 and 2.5.1, printed pages 16-17 and 26-27: a density operator is self-adjoint, nonnegative and of trace one; the general state is a convex combination of pure states

J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 6.3, printed pages 121-126: the density operator of an impure state, with the pure state |psi><psi| as the special case of complete information
G. Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (17 November 2017), Section 3.6, printed pages 95-100: trace-class operators, positivity and the trace norm

items.title: The state space is convex, closed under countable mixtures, and complete in the trace norm
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $D(H)$ be the state space of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]. Write $\mathcal S_1(H)$ for the complex Banach space of trace-class operators on $H$ with the trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$, and
$$X:=\{\rho\in\mathcal S_1(H):\rho^{*}=\rho\}$$
for the set of self-adjoint trace-class operators, regarded as a real vector space by restricting scalars from $\mathbb C$ to $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-restriction-of-scalars]], [[def-subfield]]). Then:

(a) **Finite mixtures.** $X$ is a closed real-linear subspace of $\mathcal S_1(H)$ and hence a real Banach space, and $D(H)\subseteq X$ is **closed under finite real convex combinations**, that is, it contains with any two of its points the whole real segment between them: for all $\rho,\sigma\in D(H)$ and every real $\lambda\in[0,1]$,
$$\lambda\rho+(1-\lambda)\sigma\in D(H).$$
By induction every finite convex combination $\sum_{j=1}^{n}\lambda_j\rho_j$ with $\rho_j\in D(H)$, real $\lambda_j\ge0$ and $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$ is again an element of $D(H)$.

(b) **Countable mixtures.** Let $(\rho_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq D(H)$ and let $(w_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be real weights with $w_n\ge0$ and $\sum_{n}w_n=1$. Then the series $\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$ converges absolutely in $\|\cdot\|_1$ to an element of $D(H)$: the series converges in $X$, its sum $T$ satisfies $T^{*}=T$, $T\ge0$, $\operatorname{tr}T=1$, and $\|T\|_1=\operatorname{tr}T$, with
$$\Bigl\|T-\sum_{n<K}w_n\rho_n\Bigr\|_1\longrightarrow0\quad(K\to\infty).$$

(c) **Grouping of consecutive blocks.** In the situation of (b) let $0=N_0<N_1<N_2<\cdots$ be an increasing sequence with $N_k\to\infty$, and for every $k\in\mathbb N$ put
$$u_k:=\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n,\qquad \sigma_k:=\frac{1}{u_k}\sum_{N_k\le n<N_{k+1}}w_n\rho_n,$$
where it is assumed that $u_k>0$ for every $k$ (blocks of zero weight are omitted). Then $\sigma_k\in D(H)$ for every $k$, $\sum_ku_k=1$, and
$$\sum_{k}u_k\sigma_k=\sum_{n}w_n\rho_n$$
in $\|\cdot\|_1$, the series on the left converging absolutely.

(d) **Closedness and completeness.** $D(H)$ is closed in the Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|_1)$, and $D(H)$ is complete for the trace-norm metric.
items.strategy: Direct proof that finite and countable probability mixtures of states are states, that consecutive blocks of a mixture may be grouped, and that the state space is closed and complete in the trace norm, using the trace-class Banach ideal and positivity and trace continuity.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Section 2.5.1, printed pages 26-27: the convex linear combination of two density matrices is a density matrix, and the density operators form a convex subset of the real vector space of Hermitian operators
J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 6.3, printed pages 121-124: averaging density operators with probabilities, and the trace of the averaged operator
G. Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (17 November 2017), Section 3.6, printed pages 95-100: the trace-class operators form a Banach space, with trace linear and bounded by the trace norm

items.title: Purity, spectral weights and the criterion for a pure state
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\rho\in D(H)$ be a density operator ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). Let
$$(\lambda_n)_{n\in J},\qquad J\ \text{a finite initial segment of}\ \mathbb N\ \text{or all of}\ \mathbb N,$$
be the positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ listed with multiplicity, so that $\rho=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ for an orthonormal family $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ of eigenvectors, $\rho u_n=\lambda_nu_n$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]). Then:

(a) $\lambda_n>0$ for every $n\in J$, $\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n=1$, and $\lambda_n\le1$ for every $n\in J$.

(b) $\rho^{2}$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator, and its positive eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are exactly the numbers $\lambda_n^{2}$ with $n\in J$; consequently
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=\sum_{n\in J}\lambda_n^{2}\in(0,1].$$

(c) The following four statements are equivalent: (i) $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})=1$; (ii) $J=\{n_0\}$ for a single index $n_0$ and $\lambda_{n_0}=1$; (iii) $\rho$ is a pure state; (iv) $\rho^{2}=\rho$.

(d) If $\rho$ is not pure, then $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})<1$ and $J$ contains at least two indices, so that $\rho$ has at least two positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.
items.strategy: Spectral decomposition argument: the positive eigenvalues of a state sum to one and lie in (0,1], the positive eigenvalues of the square are their squares, purity is at most one with equality exactly for the pure states, and a mixed state has at least two positive eigenvalues.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Section 2.3, printed pages 16-17: a density operator is diagonalizable with nonnegative eigenvalues summing to one, and a pure state has a single nonzero eigenvalue equal to one

G. Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 1st edition 2009, Section 6.3, printed pages 139-142 (PDF pages 151-154): spectral decomposition and the eigenvalue sum of a positive trace-class operator
G. Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (17 November 2017), Section 3.6, printed pages 96-100: the trace of a positive trace-class operator is the sum of its eigenvalues

items.title: The extreme points of the state space are exactly the pure states
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $D(H)$ be its state space ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]), regarded as a subset of the real vector space $X$ of self-adjoint trace-class operators, closed under finite real convex combinations by [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-density-set-convex-and-complete]]. Call a state $\rho\in D(H)$ an **extreme point** of $D(H)$ when
$$\rho=(1-t)\sigma+t\tau,\qquad \sigma,\tau\in D(H),\quad 0<t<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma=\tau=\rho,$$
holds for all real $t$ with $0<t<1$ and all $\sigma,\tau\in D(H)$. Then $\rho$ is an extreme point of $D(H)$ if and only if $\rho$ is a pure state.
items.strategy: Direct convexity argument: a pure state pins the quadratic forms of any convex decomposition to one and forces both components to equal it, while a mixed state is split by an explicit small perturbation of its two leading spectral terms.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Section 2.5.1, printed pages 26-27: the pure states are extremal points of the set of density matrices, and only the pure states are extremal, since every mixed state is a convex sum of pure states

J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 6.3, printed pages 121-126: a mixed state is a probability mixture of pure states, and a pure state is the special case of a single term
G. Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (17 November 2017), Section 3.6, printed pages 96-100: positive trace-class operators, their eigenvalue decompositions and their traces

items.title: The state space of the framework: preparations, pure rays and density operators
items.statement:
**(a) State space.** Adopt the state postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] for a declared system of the declared massive-matter sector, with its assigned nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $H$. The **state space of the system in the model** is the set
$$D(H)=\{\rho:\rho\ \text{is a density operator on}\ H\}$$
of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]: the self-adjoint positive trace-class operators on $H$ of trace one. A **state** of the system is an element of $D(H)$; this is the geometry vocabulary for the general preparations of clause (iii) of the state postulate. The model's adopted assignment of a state to each preparation is not produced by this definition; it is the content of that postulate.

**(b) Pure and mixed states.** A state is **pure** when it is one of the operators $T_{u,u}$ with $u\in S(H)$, and **mixed** when it is not pure, as in [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the map
$$j:R(H)\to D(H),\qquad j([\psi])=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is a bijection of the ray space onto the set of pure states; and by clause (ii) of the state postulate the pure preparations are the unit rays of $H$, so the model's pure preparations are exactly its pure states.

**(c) State assigned to a state vector.** For a nonzero vector $\psi\in H^{\times}$ the **state assigned to $\psi$** is the normalized rank-one operator
$$\widehat\rho(\psi)=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}\in D(H),$$
which by [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] depends only on the ray $[\psi]$; clause (ii) of the state postulate assigns the same operator to the pure preparation $[\psi]$. The zero vector is excluded here because $\|\psi\|^{-1}$ is defined only for $\psi\ne0$; no state is assigned to it, in agreement with the state postulate.

**(d) Mixtures and purity.** A **statistical mixture** of preparations with weights is the trace-norm convergent sum of clause (iii) of the state postulate; its value is the corresponding convex combination of states. The **purity** of a state $\rho$ is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})$, and by [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-purity-criterion]] a state is pure exactly when its purity equals $1$.

**(e) Status.** Clauses (a)-(d) record the readings of the state postulate in the geometry vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. The cited mathematical suppliers of the ray-to-state correspondence and of the purity criterion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is carried as a hypothesis of these readings. They adopt no assumption beyond the state postulate and that hypothesis, assert no dynamics, no probability law and no measurement model, and make no empirical claim: in particular, whether a given laboratory preparation is pure or mixed, and whether a given apparatus realizes a prescribed mixture, are physical identifications with uncertainty, governed by the preparation and apparatus assumptions of the framework, not consequences of this definition. Superselection restrictions and identical-particle symmetry sectors, where imposed, are separate assumptions by clause (v) of the state postulate and are not part of the state space fixed here.
items.strategy: Definition of the framework state-space vocabulary under the adopted state postulate: states as density operators, pure states as rays, the state assigned to a state vector, mixtures and purity, with the scope of the readings recorded.
items.physical_scope: The state-space vocabulary of the non-relativistic quantum framework in the declared massive-matter sector: given the state postulate's assignment of a nonzero separable complex Hilbert space and its identification of pure preparations with unit rays and general preparations with density operators, this item fixes the readings 'state space', 'state', 'pure state', 'mixed state', 'state assigned to a state vector' and 'purity', and the correspondence between pure preparations and pure states. It adds no physical assumption beyond the state postulate, asserts no dynamics, probability law, measurement model or empirical result, and excludes superselection restrictions, identical-particle sectors and all field or radiation content.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Sections 2.1 and 2.3, printed pages 3-4 and 16-18: states as rays, the density operator of an ensemble, and the convex structure of the set of states
J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Sections 1.3.4 and 6.3, printed pages 12 and 121-126: normalized states, pure states and the density operator of an impure state

items.title: Pure preparations are well defined by their rays, and phase factors do not change their states
items.statement:
Adopt the state and composition postulate P1 of the framework ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]]) and use the state-space vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the rank-one suppliers cited below. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be the Hilbert space assigned to a declared system, let $\psi,\varphi\in H^{\times}$ be nonzero state vectors, and let $[\psi],[\varphi]$ be their rays. Then:

(a) **Representative independence.** If $\varphi=z\psi$ for some nonzero $z\in\mathbb C$, then the normalized rank-one operators agree,
$$\frac{T_{\varphi,\varphi}}{\|\varphi\|^{2}}=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
and this operator is a pure state. In particular the density operator associated with a pure preparation depends only on the ray $[\psi]$ and not on the representative used to name it.

(b) **Phase invariance and injectivity.** If $u,w\in S(H)$ are unit representatives of the same ray, then $w=\zeta u$ for a unique $\zeta\in U(1)$ and $T_{w,w}=T_{u,u}$; conversely, if two pure preparations $[\psi]\ne[\varphi]$ are distinct, then their assigned pure states are distinct. Hence the assignment $[\psi]\mapsto T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}$ is a bijection from the set of pure preparations onto the set of pure states.

(c) **Exclusion of the zero vector.** The zero vector is not a pure preparation of the model: it has no unit representative, the normalization map is undefined at it, the operator $T_{0,0}=0$ has trace $0$ and is not a density operator, and the state postulate assigns pure preparations only to unit rays of vectors of norm one. Consequently no pure preparation and no state is assigned to $0$.
items.strategy: Conditional deduction from the state postulate and the mathematical state-space lemmas: representative and phase independence of the pure-state assignment, its injectivity on rays, and the exclusion of the zero vector.
items.physical_scope: A model-internal well-definedness statement about the state assignment of the non-relativistic quantum framework: with the state postulate adopted, the pure preparation of a nonzero state vector is independent of the chosen representative of its ray, phase-equivalent unit representatives yield the same pure state, distinct rays yield distinct pure states, and the zero vector is assigned no preparation or state. The item makes no empirical claim, asserts no dynamics or probability law, and does not assert that any particular laboratory procedure prepares a ray.

references.title: J. items.title: Statistical mixtures, spectral decompositions and the extremal role of pure preparations
items.statement:
Adopt the state and composition postulate P1 of the framework ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]]) and use the state-space vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the spectral and mixture suppliers cited below. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be the Hilbert space assigned to a declared system. Then:

(a) **Mixtures.** Let $(\rho_n)$ be a finite or countable family of preparations with real weights $w_n\ge0$ satisfying $\sum_nw_n=1$. Then the statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ of clause (iii) of P1 converges in trace norm to a preparation, namely to the density operator $T=\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ of [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-density-set-convex-and-complete]]. The mixture is affine in its data: a term of zero weight may be added or removed without changing $T$, and splitting one weight between two copies of the same preparation, $w\rho=w_1\rho+w_2\rho$ with $w_1+w_2=w$, leaves $T$ unchanged. If the index set is partitioned into consecutive finite blocks with total weights $u_k>0$ and block mixtures $\sigma_k$, then $\sum_ku_k\sigma_k=\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ in trace norm, so mixtures may be regrouped.

(b) **Spectral decomposition.** Every preparation $\rho$ is a countable statistical mixture of pairwise orthogonal pure preparations: there exist a finite or countable orthonormal family $(u_n)$ of unit vectors and positive weights $\lambda_n$ with $\sum_n\lambda_n=1$ such that
$$\rho=\sum_n\lambda_n\,T_{u_n,u_n},$$
the sum converging in trace norm, and the weights $\lambda_n$ are exactly the positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ counted with multiplicity.

(c) **Extremality and nontrivial decompositions.** A preparation is pure if and only if its density operator is an extreme point of the state space $D(H)$ in the sense of the condition displayed in [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-extreme-points-of-the-state-space]]; consequently every mixed preparation $\rho$ admits a representation as a statistical mixture of two preparations in a nontrivial way: if $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2>0$ are two positive eigenvalues of $\rho$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1$ and $u_2$, then with $\varepsilon:=\lambda_2/2$ the operators
$$\sigma_\pm:=\rho\pm\varepsilon\bigl(T_{u_1,u_1}-T_{u_2,u_2}\bigr)$$
are preparations with $\rho=\tfrac12\sigma_++\tfrac12\sigma_-$ and $\sigma_+\ne\sigma_-$.
items.strategy: Conditional deduction from the state postulate: well-defined affine statistical mixtures with block grouping, the spectral decomposition of every preparation into orthogonal pure preparations, and the equivalence of purity with extremality together with the explicit splitting of mixed preparations.
items.physical_scope: Model-internal statements about preparations of the non-relativistic quantum framework under the state postulate: statistical mixtures of preparations with probability weights are preparations; every preparation has a spectral decomposition as a countable mixture of pairwise orthogonal pure preparations; and the pure preparations are exactly the extreme points of the preparation set, so every mixed preparation is a nontrivial mixture of two preparations. The weights are classical preparation probabilities, not amplitudes. The item asserts no apparatus realization of any mixture, no measurement or probability law, no dynamics and no empirical result.

Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Sections 2.3 and 2.5.1, printed pages 16-18 and 26-27: the density operator of a mixture, convex combinations of density matrices, and the interpretation of convexity as an ensemble preparation

J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 6.3, printed pages 121-126: the density operator as a probability mixture of pure states, with the spectral diagonalization and the reduced-state example
G. Teschl, Topics in Real and Functional Analysis (17 November 2017), Section 3.6, printed pages 96-100: spectral decomposition of positive trace-class operators and the eigenvalue form of the trace

items.title: Scope audit of the state-geometry page: what is mathematics, what is adopted, and what is deferred
items.statement:
This remark audits the status of the items of the pair. It records which statements are conditional mathematics, which are readings of an adopted model assumption, and which questions are deliberately left to other pages. It proves nothing and asserts no empirical result.

**Mathematical layer, independent of any physical assumption.** The items [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]], [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-normalization-and-phase-classes]], [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]], [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-density-set-convex-and-complete]], [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-purity-criterion]] and [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-extreme-points-of-the-state-space]] are theorems and definitions of mathematics. They use only published or previously authored mathematical items, assume the stated choice hypotheses of those suppliers, and would be true of any complex Hilbert space regardless of any physical interpretation. In particular, the convexity of the state space, the criterion that purity is trace of the square, and the identification of the extreme points with the pure states carry no physical premise.

**The adopted state postulate is homed on the framework page.** The model assumption that a system is assigned a nonzero separable complex Hilbert space, that pure preparations are its unit rays and that general preparations are its density operators is clause-level content of [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]], authored on the framework page of this category. The present page does not restate it as a second postulate; [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]] only fixes the readings of its clauses in the geometry vocabulary, and the two physical theorems [[pthm-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-preparation-phase-invariance]] and [[pthm-nrqm-state-geometry-mixtures-and-extremal-preparations]] are conditional consequences of it together with the mathematical layer. No new physical assumption is adopted anywhere on this page.

**No observable consequence of phase is claimed here.** The two physical theorems use the redundancy of the unit representative and of phase factors only at the level of the assigned density operator. That a global phase has no consequence for any outcome probability is a statement about the framework's probability law and is not asserted on this page; the probability law, the moment conditions and the role of the phase in interferences belong to the observable and Born-probability items of this category.

**Ensembles are not determined by states.** The state postulate states, and the companion page exemplifies, that distinct weighted ensembles of pure preparations can determine the same density operator. This is a feature of the model's state assignment and not a claim that the model is incomplete, that nature is classical, or that some ensemble is the physically realized one. The mixture weights are classical preparation weights; they are not amplitudes, and no coherence between the alternatives of a mixture is asserted.

**Deliberate deferrals and exclusions.** The page adopts no superselection restriction, no identical-particle symmetry sector, no external field or radiation content and no measurement model; those are separate assumptions of the framework adopted on the pages that name them. The two-level vector space of the fixed-mode examples is treated purely as a two-dimensional Hilbert space; the identification of its vectors with photon polarization states, and any statement about photon number, energy or momentum, is deferred to the radiation assumptions of the category and is not made here.

**Empirical status.** No item of this page reports, predicts or compares a measured outcome. The worked checks of the companion page are finite computations verifying the definitions and the mathematical lemmas; they are not experiments, they use no data, and agreement of the model with any dataset is not established by them.
items.strategy: Scope audit separating the conditional mathematics, the adopted state postulate, the deferrals to later pages and the empirical neutrality of the pair.
items.physical_scope: A scope audit of the state-geometry pair: it separates the mathematical layer (rays, normalization, rank-one projections, convexity, purity and extremality of the state space) from the readings of the state postulate adopted on the framework page, records that this page adopts no new physical assumption and no empirical claim, and lists the deliberate deferrals: observable consequences of phase, the probability law, measurement models, superselection and identical-particle sectors, and the photon interpretation of two-level polarization vectors. The remark proves nothing and asserts no observation.

J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 6.3, printed pages 121-126: pure and impure states, and the remark that an impure state is not a pure state with unknown parameters

items.title: A two-dimensional normalization and phase computation
items.statement:
Let $H=\mathbb C^{2}$ carry the standard inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle=z_{1}\overline{w_{1}}+z_{2}\overline{w_{2}}$$
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]; completeness follows from [[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]]), and let $e_{1}=(1,0)$, $e_{2}=(0,1)$. Take
$$\psi=(1,i),\qquad z=1+i,\qquad \varphi:=z\psi,$$
and verify on this explicit data the normalization and phase statements of [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-normalization-and-phase-classes]]: the norm of $\varphi$ is $|z|$ times the norm of $\psi$, the normalized representative of $\varphi$ is the phase multiple $(z/|z|)$ of the normalized representative of $\psi$, the rays of $\psi$ and $\varphi$ coincide, and the normalized rank-one operators of $\psi$, $\varphi$ and $i\psi$ are the same pure state [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]].
items.strategy: Worked two-dimensional computation verifying normalization, phase classes and representative independence of the pure state on the explicit vectors (1,i) and (1+i)(1,i).

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Sections 2.1 and 2.2.1, printed pages 4 and 8-9: normalized representatives of rays, the phase redundancy of |psi> and the qubit state |psi(phi,theta)> = (e^{-i phi/2} cos(theta/2), e^{i phi/2} sin(theta/2))
J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 1.3.4 and 1.3.5, printed pages 12-13: normalization of a two-component state and the role of relative phase

items.title: The state space of a two-level finite-spin system is the Bloch ball
items.statement:
Consider the model's two-level finite-spin assignment: the internal space $H=\mathbb C^{2}$ of a spin-one-half system ([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]), with the standard inner product and the Pauli matrices
$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$
of [[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clause (e). For $r=(r_1,r_2,r_3)\in\mathbb R^{3}$ write $r\cdot\sigma=r_1\sigma_x+r_2\sigma_y+r_3\sigma_z$ and $|r|^{2}=r_1^{2}+r_2^{2}+r_3^{2}$. Then, using the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]:

(i) A linear operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a state if and only if there is $r\in\mathbb R^{3}$ with
$$\rho=\frac12\bigl(I+r\cdot\sigma\bigr)\qquad\text{and}\qquad |r|\le1;$$
that is, the state space is the unit ball of $\mathbb R^{3}$ in this parametrization.

(ii) Such a state is pure if and only if $|r|=1$; and if $|r|=1$ and $\psi$ is a unit eigenvector of $r\cdot\sigma$ with eigenvalue $1$, then $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$.

(iii) The value $r=0$ gives the mixed state $\tfrac12I$ of purity $\tfrac12$, and $r=e_3=(0,0,1)$ gives the pure state $\tfrac12(I+\sigma_z)=T_{e_1,e_1}$ with $e_1=(1,0)$.
items.strategy: Worked finite computation parametrizing the two-level state space by the Bloch ball (I+r.sigma)/2, testing positivity by an explicit projection decomposition and purity by the trace of the square.
items.physical_scope: A worked computation in the model's two-level finite-spin state space: for the spin-one-half assignment of the framework, the density operators on the two-dimensional internal space are exactly the operators (I + r dot sigma)/2 with |r| <= 1, and the pure states are exactly the boundary points |r| = 1, each of which is the rank-one state of the corresponding spin-up ray. The Bloch ball is a parametrization of the model's states; the item asserts no measurement outcome probability, no experimental result and no interpretation of r beyond the displayed formula.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Section 2.3.2, printed pages 21-23: the general qubit density matrix rho = (I + P dot sigma)/2, det rho = (1 - P^2)/4, the Bloch ball and its boundary as the pure states

B. Zwiebach, MIT 8.05 Quantum Physics II (Fall 2013), Chapter 2 'Spin One-Half, Bras, Kets, and Operators', Sections 1-3, printed pages 1-16: the Pauli matrices, spin states and the density operator of a spin-one-half system
J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 7.4.2, printed pages 161-164: the spin-one-half operators and their matrices

items.title: Pure and mixed states of a fixed two-level internal space
items.statement:
Let $H$ be a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space with an orthonormal basis written $(h,v)$, and use the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. Put
$$u:=\frac{h+v}{\sqrt2}\in S(H),\qquad \rho_+:=\frac12T_{h,h}+\frac12T_{v,v},$$
the first the ray of the equal-amplitude superposition of the two basis vectors, the second the equal statistical mixture of the two basis rays. Then:

(i) The state assigned to the ray $[u]$ is the pure state $T_{u,u}$, whose matrix relative to the basis $(h,v)$ is
$$T_{u,u}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 1&1\end{pmatrix};$$
its purity is $1$ and its rank is one.

(ii) The mixture is the state $\rho_+=\frac12I$, whose matrix relative to $(h,v)$ is diagonal with entries $\frac12$; its purity is $\frac12$, it is mixed, and it is not a pure state.

(iii) The two states are distinct: $T_{u,u}\ne\frac12I$, and they differ in rank and in purity.

The basis labels $h$ and $v$ are abstract here. The identification of such a two-level space with the polarization states of a fixed propagation mode, and every statement about photon number, energy, momentum or detection, is deferred to the radiation assumptions adopted on the radiation pages of the category; no such identification or statement is made in this item.
items.strategy: Worked computation of the pure state of a diagonal vector and of the equal statistical mixture in an abstract two-level space with a polarization basis, with the photon reading deferred.
items.physical_scope: A worked computation in a fixed two-dimensional internal space carrying an orthonormal pair of 'polarization' labels: the state of the diagonal vector is the pure state with matrix (1/2)[[1,1],[1,1]], and the equal statistical mixture of the two basis labels is the mixed state (1/2)I. The two-level space is treated abstractly; the identification of its vectors with photon polarization states, and any statement about photon number, energy or momentum, is deferred to the radiation assumptions of the category and is not made in this item. The item asserts no measurement probability and no empirical result.

references.title: J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 1.3.6, printed pages 14-15: two orthonormal basis states of a fixed photon polarization mode, the superposition with equal amplitudes, and the transmission probabilities for a rotated analyser

J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Section 2.2.2, printed pages 14-16: photon polarization states as a two-dimensional internal space with orthonormal basis {|x>,|y>}

items.title: A coherent two-level preparation and the equal statistical mixture are different states
items.statement:
Let $H$ be a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space with orthonormal basis $(h,v)$, and use the state space $D(H)$ and the preparation semantics of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. Consider the two preparations
$$\text{superposition:}\quad w=\frac{h+iv}{\sqrt2},\qquad\qquad \text{equal mixture:}\quad \rho_+=\frac12T_{h,h}+\frac12T_{v,v},$$
where $w$ is a unit vector and $\rho_+$ is the statistical mixture of the two basis rays with weights $\frac12,\frac12$. Then the assigned states are
$$T_{w,w}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\ i&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \rho_+=\frac12 I,$$
and they are distinct states of the model: $T_{w,w}$ is pure with purity $1$ and rank one, while $\rho_+$ is mixed with purity $\frac12$ and rank two. In particular the relative phase of the superposition is not erased at the level of the assigned state, and the superposition and the mixture are not the same preparation.
items.strategy: Worked comparison of a relative-phase superposition with the equal mixture: the two assigned matrices differ in rank and purity, so the preparations are distinct states.
items.physical_scope: A worked comparison, inside the framework's state space, of two preparations of a two-level system: the pure preparation of the relative-phase superposition (h + i v)/sqrt2 and the equal statistical mixture of the h and v rays. The two assigned states are computed explicitly and shown to be distinct, with different rank and purity: the superposition is pure and the mixture is mixed. The item asserts no outcome probability, no measurement model, no apparatus realization and no empirical result; the relative-phase (coherence) comparison at the level of outcome statistics belongs to the framework's probability law and is not made here.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Sections 2.2.1 and 2.3, printed pages 8-12 and 16-19: superpositions with a relative phase versus incoherent mixtures, and their different density matrices

J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Sections 1.3.5 and 6.3, printed pages 12-13 and 121-126: the role of relative phase in superpositions and the distinction between a superposition and a probability mixture embodied in the density operator

items.title: One two-level state from two different preparation ensembles
items.statement:
Let $H$ be a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space with orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2)$ and use the state space and preparation semantics of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. Let $\rho$ be the diagonal state
$$\rho=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&0\\ 0&1/4\end{pmatrix}$$
relative to $(e_1,e_2)$, and put
$$\psi=\Bigl(\cos\frac\pi6,\ \sin\frac\pi6\Bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\Bigr),\qquad \varphi=\Bigl(\cos\frac\pi6,\ -\sin\frac\pi6\Bigr)=\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\Bigr).$$
Then:

(i) $\rho=\frac34T_{e_1,e_1}+\frac14T_{e_2,e_2}$: the projective (orthonormal) ensemble with weights $\frac34,\frac14$.

(ii) $\rho=\frac12T_{\psi,\psi}+\frac12T_{\varphi,\varphi}$: the uniform ensemble of the two pure preparations $[\psi]$ and $[\varphi]$, which are not orthogonal, since
$$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle=\cos^{2}\frac\pi6-\sin^{2}\frac\pi6=\frac34-\frac14=\frac12\ne0 .$$

(iii) The two ensembles differ in their members and in their weights, yet they determine the same preparation, whose purity is $\frac34^{2}+\frac14^{2}=\frac58<1$. Hence the assigned state does not determine the ensemble, and two distinct statistical preparations may determine the same state.
items.strategy: Worked computation exhibiting one mixed two-level state as an orthonormal ensemble with unequal weights and as the uniform mixture of two non-orthogonal pure states.
items.physical_scope: A worked computation in the framework's two-level state space showing that two distinct statistical mixtures of pure preparations, with different members and different weights, determine the same mixed preparation: the diagonal state with eigenvalues 3/4 and 1/4 arises both as the orthonormal spectral ensemble with weights 3/4, 1/4 and as the uniform mixture of two non-orthogonal pure states. The item shows that the state does not determine the ensemble; it asserts no measurement probability, no apparatus realization and no empirical result, and it makes no claim of physical incompleteness.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Sections 2.5.1-2.5.2 and 2.5.5, printed pages 26-29 and 34-36: the ambiguity of the ensemble interpretation and the ensemble preparation of convex combinations

J. Binney and D. Skinner, The Physics of Quantum Mechanics, Section 6.3, printed pages 121-125: the density operator of a mixture in two different bases, and the non-uniqueness of the expansion of a density operator

items.title: The zero vector determines no pure preparation and no state
items.statement: Adopt the state postulate of the framework, and let $H\ne\{0\}$ be the Hilbert space assigned to a declared system. Then: **every** vector of $H$ determines a pure preparation of the system; the zero vector determines the zero operator $0$, which is the state of the system when no preparation is made, and the normalization convention $0/\|0\|=0$ supplies the unit representative of its ray.
items.strategy: Direct refutation of the claim that every vector determines a pure preparation: no unit representative exists for the zero vector, the normalization is undefined, and the zero operator is not a density operator.
items.physical_scope: A refutation, inside the framework's state semantics, of the claim that every vector of the assigned Hilbert space determines a pure preparation with the zero vector corresponding to the zero operator: the zero vector has no unit representative, the normalization map is undefined at it, and the zero operator has trace zero and is not a density operator, so under the state postulate no preparation and no state is assigned to it. The item refutes that specific informal claim; it asserts no empirical result and no claim about nature.

references.title: J. Preskill, Lecture Notes for Ph219/CS219: Quantum Information, Chapter 2 (updated July 2015), Section 2.1, printed page 4: positivity of the inner product is stated for |psi> not equal to 0, and a ray is an equivalence class of nonzero vectors
G. Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 1st edition 2009, Section 2.1, printed pages 55-56 (PDF pages 66-67): the states are the vectors of norm one, so the zero vector is not a state

items.title: What the worked checks of the companion page establish
items.statement:
This remark audits the companion page. It records what each item computes, and what none of them claims. It proves nothing and reports no observation.

**Elementary normalization and phase.** [[ex-nrqm-state-geometry-normalization-and-phase-check]] computes, on the explicit two-dimensional data $\psi=(1,i)$ and $\varphi=(1+i)\psi$, the norms, the normalized representatives, the phase relating them and the normalized rank-one operators; it verifies the normalization and phase class lemma of the main page and exhibits the representative independence of the pure state on a worked vector pair.

**Finite spin and the two-level state space.** [[ex-nrqm-state-geometry-finite-spin-bloch-ball]] proves that the states of the model's two-level finite-spin system are exactly the operators $\frac12(I+r\cdot\sigma)$ with $|r|\le1$, that the pure states are the boundary points $|r|=1$, and that each boundary point is the rank-one state of the corresponding spin-up ray. [[ex-nrqm-state-geometry-fixed-mode-two-level-states]] repeats the corresponding elementary computation for an abstract two-level internal space carrying a pair of polarization labels, showing the pure state of the diagonal vector and the equal mixture of the basis rays. Neither item asserts the identification of the abstract two-level space with photon polarization; that reading belongs to the radiation assumptions of the category, and no statement about photon number, energy or momentum is made here.

**Superposition versus mixture, and non-unique ensembles.** [[ex-nrqm-state-geometry-coherent-versus-mixed-preparation]] shows that the relative-phase superposition $(h+iv)/\sqrt2$ and the equal statistical mixture of the rays $[h]$ and $[v]$ are assigned different states, with different rank and purity, so the two preparations are not the same. [[ex-nrqm-state-geometry-nonunique-preparation-ensembles]] shows the converse direction of freedom: one and the same mixed state is determined by two genuinely different ensembles, an orthonormal pair with unequal weights and a uniform pair of non-orthogonal states. Both computations stop at the level of the assigned states; which outcome probabilities distinguish states, and with which apparatus, is the subject of the framework's probability law and measurement assumptions.

**Zero-vector exclusion.** [[cex-nrqm-state-geometry-zero-vector-is-not-a-preparation]] refutes the informal claim that every vector determines a pure preparation with the zero vector as an empty preparation: the zero vector has no unit representative, the normalization map is undefined at it, and the zero operator has trace zero and is not a state. The refutation concerns the model's definitions and assignment; it is not an experiment and it makes no claim about nature.

**Empirical neutrality.** Every item of this page is a finite computation or the refutation just described. None of them uses measured data, none adopts a law of nature, none predicts the outcome of any measurement, and none compares a model prediction with an observation. Agreement or disagreement with data would test the combined framework and apparatus assumptions, and is not established or claimed here.
items.strategy: Scope audit of the companion page: what each finite check verifies and the empirical neutrality of all of them.
items.physical_scope: A scope audit of the companion page of worked checks: it records what each computation verifies, that all of them are finite state-space computations or one refutation of an informal claim about the model's state semantics, and that none is an experiment, a measurement prediction or a comparison with data.
